paragraphs: Fine-tuning large language models can require more memory than researchers have available. Block coordinate descent reduces this burden by dividing parameters into blocks and training one block while holding the others fixed. This paper identifies two reasons that applying this strategy directly to language models can make training inefficient.

First, updating the active block still requires backward computation through deeper, frozen blocks, leaving some of that computation underused. Second, frozen blocks that are far from their best settings can restrict the possibilities available to the active block and potentially steer its training poorly. The proposed landscape expansion method updates those inactive blocks cheaply during the same backward pass used for the active block.

Experiments on models with 8 billion and 70 billion parameters show better results than the memory-efficient baselines tested. The method matches Adam’s downstream performance while using 24 GB and 300 GB of memory, respectively. These findings support updating otherwise frozen blocks as a way to improve the usefulness of memory-constrained training.
neurips-2025-accelerating-block-coordina.tldr: Landscape expansion makes block coordinate fine-tuning more effective by cheaply updating inactive blocks during the existing backward pass.

paragraphs: Differentially private training bounds individual examples’ contributions by clipping their gradients, the directions used to update a model. Conventional clipping shrinks gradients by different amounts depending on their size. When these gradients are combined, that unequal shrinking can change the direction of the overall update relative to the original batch gradient.

Shrinking every gradient by the same small factor helps preserve direction, but it can make the combined update excessively weak. AdaSig addresses this direction–magnitude trade-off using a sigmoid function whose saturation slope can change during training. Adjusting the slope lets the clipping rule respond as the distribution of sample gradients evolves, rather than using the same balance throughout learning.

The authors show that DP-SGD with this adaptive clipping rule retains the best-known convergence rate for non-convex losses. On the sentence and image classification datasets evaluated, AdaSig consistently improves learning performance over established clipping methods. The contribution therefore combines an adaptive way to manage clipping distortion with a convergence result and empirical evidence of better classification performance.
neurips-2025-adaptive-sigmoid-clipping-f.tldr: AdaSig adaptively balances changes to gradient direction and magnitude during private training, improving tested classification results while retaining the best-known convergence rate.

paragraphs: Language-model agents often receive instructions containing extensive operating rules, tool descriptions, and conditions governing their behavior. AgentIF tests whether models actually follow these requirements in realistic agent settings. Its focus is instruction adherence when a task involves many interacting constraints, a capability that existing agent demonstrations do not by themselves establish.

The benchmark contains 707 human-annotated instructions drawn from 50 real-world agentic applications and tasks, including industrial and open-source systems. Instructions average 1,723 words and reach 15,630 words, with an average of 11.9 constraints each. The authors annotate individual constraints and assign evaluation procedures using code, language-model judgments, or combinations of both.

The evaluated advanced models generally perform poorly, particularly on complex constraint structures and tool specifications. Additional analyses examine errors, instruction length, and meta constraints to investigate failure patterns. These findings make the benchmark useful for distinguishing an agent’s apparent task competence from its ability to obey detailed operating instructions, while grounding that assessment in requirements collected from actual applications.
neurips-2025-agentif-benchmarking-large-.tldr: AgentIF exposes weaknesses in advanced language models’ ability to follow long, complex instructions drawn from real agent applications.

paragraphs: Autoformalization translates ordinary mathematical writing into a formal language that machines can check. Training models for this task requires paired informal and formal statements, but such examples are scarce. ATLAS addresses that data bottleneck by generating a large parallel collection of theorem statements, making data construction central to improving the translator.

The framework starts from a repository of concepts and improves a student model through expert iteration and knowledge distillation. It also introduces two augmentation strategies that use the structure of formal languages. After 10 iterations, the authors produce 117,000 undergraduate-level theorem statements and train the ATLAS Translator by applying LoRA fine-tuning to Llama3.1-8B-Instruct.

The translator outperforms Herald Translator and Kimina-Autoformalizer across all evaluated benchmarks, with statistically significant differences under the reported two-sided t-tests. Full-parameter fine-tuning of a stronger base model on the same dataset delivers further improvement. Together, these results support the value of ATLAS’s generated training data for translating theorem statements, including when paired with a more capable underlying model.
neurips-2025-atlas-autoformalizing-theor.tldr: ATLAS generates paired informal and formal theorem statements that improve mathematical autoformalization across the evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: BTL-UI addresses how an AI agent organizes its interaction with a graphical interface. The paper argues that existing agents’ interaction logic differs substantially from natural human interaction patterns. Its Blink–Think–Link framework uses a brain-inspired sequence to connect attention to relevant screen content, reasoning about what to do, and execution of interface actions.

Blink rapidly identifies relevant screen regions, drawing an analogy with eye movements. Think handles higher-level planning and decisions. Link turns those decisions into executable commands for precise interaction. To support training, the authors introduce an automated annotation pipeline tailored to Blink data and a rule-based reward mechanism that evaluates both the interaction process and its outcome.

The resulting BTL-UI model achieves competitive performance on benchmarks covering static interface understanding and dynamic interaction. This evidence supports the usefulness of the three-phase organization for building GUI agents. The contribution includes both the interaction framework and the data-generation and reward components needed to train agents around that framework.
neurips-2025-btl-ui-blink-think-link-rea.tldr: BTL-UI organizes GUI interaction into visual attention, reasoning, and command execution, supported by automated annotations and rewards for process and outcome.

paragraphs: Recent reasoning improvements from reinforcement learning have largely been demonstrated in language models that generate text from left to right. Diffusion language models instead generate text through coarse-to-fine refinement. This paper asks whether pretrained masked diffusion models can also benefit from the post-training techniques that have strengthened reasoning in autoregressive models.

The proposed d1 framework combines supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning. Its masked supervised training transfers knowledge from existing datasets and encourages self-improvement behavior. The authors also introduce diffu-GRPO, a policy-gradient reinforcement-learning algorithm that does not require a critic. This supplies a way to apply policy-gradient training within the masked diffusion generation setting.

Experiments compare different post-training recipes across mathematical and planning benchmarks. Among the recipes studied, d1 performs best and significantly improves the performance of a state-of-the-art diffusion language model. The findings provide empirical support for improving diffusion-model reasoning through combined supervised and reinforcement learning, extending the demonstrated usefulness of these techniques beyond left-to-right text generation.
neurips-2025-d1-scaling-reasoning-in-dif.tldr: d1 combines masked supervised fine-tuning with critic-free reinforcement learning to improve diffusion language models on mathematical and planning tasks.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models face substantial memory and storage costs as their collections of experts grow. Removing experts can reduce those costs, but applying the same pruning rate to every layer overlooks differences in redundancy. A layer with many dispensable experts may tolerate more pruning than one whose experts contribute more distinctly.

DiEP learns different pruning rates for different layers while jointly accounting for importance across layers. Choosing which experts to retain is a discrete search problem with exponentially many possible combinations. The method converts that search into a continuous form, allowing gradients to guide the pruning decisions and adapt the allocation of retained experts.

Experiments cover five MoE models and multiple language tasks. On Mixtral 8×7B, DiEP retains around 92% of the original performance with half the experts and outperforms other pruning methods by up to 7.1% on MMLU. These results support adapting compression to layer-specific redundancy rather than imposing a uniform pruning rate throughout a model.
neurips-2025-diep-adaptive-mixture-of-ex.tldr: DiEP learns layer-specific expert pruning rates, retaining around 92% of Mixtral 8×7B’s original performance with half its experts.

paragraphs: Adapting a large language model remains costly even when only a small adapter is trained. This paper frames adaptation as aligning the model’s output distribution with a task’s distribution. Steering Vector Decoding, or SVDecode, uses that perspective to guide generation directly, complementing parameter-efficient fine-tuning with a change to decoding.

The method first performs a short warm-start fine-tune. It then derives a task-aware steering vector from the gradient of KL divergence between the warm-started and pretrained models’ output distributions. That vector guides subsequent decoding. The authors prove first-order equivalence to a full fine-tuning gradient step and derive a globally optimal steering strength within their formulation.

Across three tasks and nine benchmarks, combining SVDecode with four standard parameter-efficient methods improves multiple-choice accuracy by up to five percentage points and open-ended truthfulness by two points. Commonsense gains are one to two points. These improvements require no additional trainable parameters beyond the adapter, supporting decoding-time steering as a lightweight addition to task adaptation.
neurips-2025-distribution-aligned-decodi.tldr: SVDecode derives a task-aware vector from a short fine-tune and uses it during decoding to improve adaptation without extra trainable parameters.

paragraphs: Robotic manipulation requires visually guided actions that are both precise and efficient to compute. FreqPolicy approaches this challenge through the representation of motion. The authors observe that frequency components separate broad movement patterns from finer local details, creating a structured way to model the actions a robot should take.

Low-frequency components describe the overall movement, while high-frequency components capture finer variations. Because manipulation tasks differ in complexity, they can require different levels of precision across these components. FreqPolicy progressively models this frequency hierarchy using an autoregressive framework. It also introduces continuous latent representations to preserve smoothness and continuity in the action space while improving precision.

Experiments across diverse two-dimensional and three-dimensional manipulation benchmarks show better accuracy and efficiency than the existing methods evaluated. These findings support frequency-based action modeling as a useful design for visuomotor policies. The contribution brings together a hierarchical description of motion and continuous action representations, with the reported results indicating benefits for both precise control and computational efficiency.
neurips-2025-freqpolicy-frequency-autore.tldr: FreqPolicy progressively models robot actions across frequency bands with continuous representations, improving accuracy and efficiency on evaluated manipulation benchmarks.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning has strengthened language-model reasoning, but much of that work concentrates on mathematics and coding. Those fields offer abundant questions and relatively convenient ways to check answers. General-Reasoner targets broader disciplines, where data can be scarcer and correct answers may appear in varied forms that are difficult to evaluate with fixed rules.

The framework addresses both training data and answer verification. The authors curate a large collection of questions with verifiable answers through web crawling across disciplines. They also build a generative answer verifier that uses reasoning and context, replacing traditional rule-based checks. This pairing supplies broader material for learning and a more flexible way to assess responses.

The authors train a series of models and evaluate them on 12 benchmarks spanning fields such as physics, chemistry, finance, and electronics. General-Reasoner outperforms the baseline methods evaluated while also maintaining strong mathematical reasoning performance. The results support broadening reinforcement-learning-based reasoning through diverse verifiable questions and context-aware assessment, with evidence across the tested domains.
neurips-2025-general-reasoner-advancing-.tldr: General-Reasoner combines diverse verifiable questions with a context-aware answer verifier to improve reasoning across the evaluated disciplines.

paragraphs: In incentivized exploration, a principal learns by interacting with successive agents who pursue their own interests. The learning strategy must give those agents reasons to follow its recommendations. A central difficulty is collecting enough initial information: once a moderate amount is available, posterior sampling can achieve near-optimal regret, measuring losses relative to better choices.

With high-dimensional contexts, this initial exploration can require exponentially many samples in some settings. The paper shows that this obstacle disappears under mild geometric conditions on the available actions. It studies a linear bandit setting whose actions lie in the Euclidean unit ball, making the geometry of the choices central to the result.

For this setting, the authors construct an incentive-compatible exploration algorithm whose sample requirement grows polynomially with dimension and other parameters. The finding establishes that respecting agents’ incentives need not prevent regret-optimal learning under the stated geometric conditions. It also identifies action-space structure as a reason some initial exploration problems can be tractable despite the difficulties found in other high-dimensional settings.
neurips-2025-geometry-meets-incentives-s.tldr: Under suitable action-space geometry, incentive-compatible linear-bandit exploration needs polynomially many initial samples rather than facing exponential barriers.

paragraphs: Human ratings are important for evaluating generative models, but the available ratings can have two complications at once. Some interactions receive no annotation, and interactions within a group can be correlated. For example, questions from the same user may resemble one another, so their ratings cannot simply be treated as independent observations.

This paper studies estimation of average annotation scores when both missing responses and cluster dependence are present. It analyzes the doubly robust estimator, an established method in missing-data analysis and causal inference, and develops theoretical properties for this dependent setting. The goal is to address bias in the estimated average while also quantifying its uncertainty appropriately.

The authors illustrate their theoretical findings with simulations and a real-world dataset of conversation quality. Their combined results emphasize that handling missing annotations alone is insufficient for valid inference when clustered dependence also matters. The contribution provides a statistical foundation for evaluating average human scores while taking the grouping of interactions seriously in the analysis.
neurips-2025-handling-missing-responses-.tldr: The paper develops theory for estimating average human evaluation scores when annotations are missing and interactions are correlated within clusters.

paragraphs: Knowledge graphs organize entities and their relationships, but keeping them current becomes difficult as scientific literature expands. KARMA automates enrichment by turning unstructured documents into additions to an existing graph. Its focus includes extracting information, checking it, and making it fit the rules and structure of the target domain.

The framework uses nine collaborating language-model agents with responsibilities spanning entity discovery, relation extraction, schema alignment, and conflict resolution. They repeatedly analyze documents, verify candidate knowledge, and integrate it into the graph. This division of work treats enrichment as a sequence of coordinated judgments, including whether a proposed addition is consistent with the graph’s domain-specific schema.

Experiments use 1,200 PubMed articles from three domains. KARMA identifies up to 38,230 new entities, reports 83.1% correctness as verified by LLMs, and reduces conflicting edges by 18.6% through layered assessments. These findings demonstrate substantial automated enrichment in the evaluated material, with the correctness figure specifically reflecting model-based verification and the conflict result showing the contribution of consistency assessment.
neurips-2025-karma-leveraging-multi-agen.tldr: KARMA coordinates nine language-model agents to extract, verify, and integrate scientific knowledge into existing graphs.

paragraphs: Kernel ridge regression theory commonly assumes that training observations are independent and identically distributed. This assumption does not describe settings where several noisy observations come from the same underlying signal. Such observations share information, making their dependence important for understanding how well a learned model will generalize beyond its training data.

The paper studies this signal–noise structure directly. Under standard assumptions about the decay of the kernel spectrum, the authors develop a blockwise decomposition that makes concentration analysis possible for dependent observations. They derive excess-risk bounds that account for the spectrum, the causal structure linking signals and noise, and how samples are collected.

The bounds explicitly include the relative numbers of underlying signals and noisy observations. This matters because sampling more noisy views and sampling more distinct signals affect the structure of the data differently. Applying the analysis to denoising score learning yields generalization guarantees and principled guidance for sampling noisy points, connecting the theoretical treatment of dependence to a concrete learning application.
neurips-2025-kernel-regression-in-struct.tldr: The paper derives kernel-regression generalization bounds for noisy views of shared signals and applies them to denoising score learning.

paragraphs: An AI system and its user can reach different conclusions because their internal models differ. Model reconciliation explains which changes would bring those models into agreement. This paper extends that idea to uncertain knowledge, addressing a gap in approaches that primarily assume deterministic models and therefore do not represent probabilistic differences directly.

The framework represents the agent’s and user’s models using ProbLog, a probabilistic logic programming system. It targets disagreements in MPE outcome probabilities and constructs explanations as model updates that resolve those differences at minimum cost. This makes explanation generation a search over changes to the model, with reconciliation and update cost defining the objective.

The authors develop a generic search baseline and an optimized algorithm guided by theoretical insights. Greedy and weighted variants further address efficiency and scalability. A user study examines explanation types, while computational experiments show that the optimized algorithm consistently outperforms the generic baseline. The work provides both a probabilistic formulation of reconciliation and algorithms for finding the corresponding explanatory updates.
neurips-2025-model-reconciliation-via-co.tldr: The framework explains probabilistic disagreements between an AI and a user through cost-optimal updates to their logic-based models.

paragraphs: This paper develops an entropic-force theory to explain learning dynamics in neural networks trained with stochastic gradient descent and related methods. The theory connects parameter symmetries with an entropic view of the loss landscape. It attributes emergent forces shaping representations to both randomness in training and updates occurring in discrete steps.

The authors show that these forces break continuous parameter symmetries while preserving discrete ones. The resulting gradient-balance phenomena resemble equipartition in thermal systems. This provides the bridge between the paper’s physical interpretation and its account of how neural representations develop: the structure of parameter symmetries interacts with the dynamics of the training procedure.

The theory is used to explain alignment between representations learned by different AI models and to establish a proof of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis within its theoretical treatment. It also reconciles observations that optimization can favor either sharp or flat regions of the loss landscape. Together, the theory and experiments support entropic forces and symmetry breaking as mechanisms for understanding these emergent learning phenomena.
neurips-2025-neural-thermodynamics-entro.tldr: The paper develops an entropic-force theory linking training dynamics and parameter symmetries to representation alignment and sharpness-versus-flatness behavior.

paragraphs: Internet protocol specifications describe states and the events or actions that connect them, but extracting this structure from dense RFC text remains difficult. PSMBench evaluates whether language models can turn those documents into machine-readable protocol state machines. Such extraction matters for automated protocol testing and security analysis that depend on the resulting graph.

The accompanying RFC2PSM dataset pairs 1,580 pages of cleaned text with 108 manually validated states and 297 transitions across 14 deployed protocols. The benchmark supplies RFC text in chunks, asks a model to produce a state machine, and scores it with structure-aware semantic matching. Its metrics give credit for partially correct graphs rather than requiring exact textual agreement.

Testing nine open and commercial models reveals a substantial gap between recognizing states and connecting them correctly. State identification reaches 0.82 F1, while transition scores remain at or below 0.38 F1. The results highlight difficulties with long-context reasoning, alternate names, and distinctions between actions and events, showing that identifying components does not establish coherent protocol reconstruction.
neurips-2025-psmbench-a-benchmark-and-da.tldr: PSMBench shows that tested language models recognize protocol states much better than they reconstruct the transitions connecting them.

paragraphs: RadZero learns connections between chest X-rays and radiology text to support classification, localization, and segmentation without task-specific training examples at inference. It addresses two challenges: extracting useful information from complex reports and making image–text alignment more interpretable. Language models first turn reports into concise semantic sentences for training.

The framework uses multi-positive contrastive training so an image can be associated with several relevant descriptions. A pretrained vision encoder and additional trainable Transformer layers support efficient processing of high-resolution images. Its central component, VL-CABS, compares text embeddings with local image features, tying textual descriptions to particular parts of the X-ray.

Those similarities provide classification probabilities and pixel-level maps for grounding and segmentation. On public chest-radiograph benchmarks, RadZero outperforms state-of-the-art methods in the three zero-shot tasks evaluated. Map analysis suggests potential for better explainability, while qualitative examples demonstrate open-vocabulary semantic segmentation. These findings connect the same local similarity mechanism to both task performance and spatially interpretable image–text associations.
neurips-2025-radzero-similarity-based-cr.tldr: RadZero aligns report-derived text with local X-ray features to improve zero-shot classification, grounding, and segmentation while producing interpretable similarity maps.

paragraphs: Temporal graph neural networks combine reasoning about graph structure with reasoning about changes over time. This paper studies their expressive power through logic: which properties of an evolving graph can an architecture represent? It connects temporal GNNs to two-dimensional product logics that describe both the spatial and temporal aspects of the data.

The key finding is that expressive power depends on how the graph and time components are combined. Architectures that recursively apply static GNNs over time can capture every property definable in the product of past propositional temporal logic and modal logic K. This gives a formal capability result for that particular architectural organization.

Other architectures, including graph-and-time TGNNs and global TGNNs, express only restricted fragments of this logic. In those fragments, syntax constrains how temporal and spatial operators interact. The results establish initial logical characterizations of temporal GNNs and make architectural differences precise: combining graph and temporal processing in different ways changes the kinds of joint properties a model can express.
neurips-2025-the-logical-expressiveness-.tldr: The paper uses product logics to show how the combination of graph and temporal processing determines temporal GNN expressiveness.

paragraphs: FP8 formats offer potential speed advantages for language-model pretraining, but maintaining numerical stability at scale is difficult. Existing approaches may use less efficient fine-grained kernels or retain higher precision for sensitive matrix multiplications, including attention projections. These compromises reduce the throughput gains that low-precision computation could otherwise provide.

The paper introduces architectures that support FP8 for every matrix multiplication inside Transformer blocks during both forward and backward passes. The architecture design reduces unusually large activations, which helps sustain stable training over long runs. This addresses stability through the model’s structure while expanding where FP8 computation can be used.

The authors report substantial throughput improvements, especially at scale, while matching the downstream performance of standard BF16 training. They also identify monitoring metrics that can signal potential future training divergence. The contribution therefore combines an architecture that supports broader low-precision computation with tools for tracking its stability, specifically covering matrix multiplications within Transformer blocks rather than claiming every training operation uses FP8.
neurips-2025-towards-fully-fp8-gemm-llm-.tldr: New architectures stabilize FP8 matrix multiplications throughout Transformer blocks, improving training throughput while matching BF16 downstream performance.

paragraphs: Tree ensembles can predict tabular outcomes accurately while remaining difficult to interpret. The Hoeffding functional decomposition offers a way to separate a model into contributions from individual variables and their interactions. With independent inputs, this decomposition is unique. Dependent inputs require a generalization based on hierarchical orthogonality to define those effects distinctly.

Although the generalized decomposition can be unique and sparse, estimating it from sampled data is a practical challenge. TreeHFD addresses this problem specifically for tree ensembles. The authors establish convergence and properties involving orthogonality, sparsity, and causal variable selection, giving theoretical support to the algorithm’s reconstruction of the model’s component effects.

Experiments on simulated and real data demonstrate strong performance using the authors’ Python implementation. The paper also finds an empirical connection between the widely used TreeSHAP method and the Hoeffding decomposition. Together, these contributions provide a practical route to separating main effects from interactions and relate that decomposition-based explanation to an established approach based on Shapley values.
neurips-2025-tree-ensemble-explainabilit.tldr: TreeHFD estimates a tree ensemble’s Hoeffding decomposition, separating main effects and interactions while accommodating dependent inputs.

paragraphs: Numerical solutions of partial differential equations balance accuracy against computation. Moving mesh nodes toward regions where the solution varies rapidly can improve that balance. Traditional movement methods can be expensive and geometrically inflexible, while supervised learned methods face difficulties transferring to unfamiliar equations and mesh structures without additional training.

UGM2N learns mesh adaptation without requiring pre-adapted meshes as training targets. It uses local geometric features and a physics-constrained objective called M-Uniform loss. This loss enforces equidistribution at the level of individual nodes, providing a training signal for how mesh points should be arranged. The approach connects unsupervised learning to a physically constrained mesh-adaptation criterion.

The reported experiments show generalization across equations and geometries, alongside efficient adaptation and scalability across resolutions. The abstract also reports consistent superiority over existing methods, guaranteed error reduction, and avoidance of mesh tangling. These findings support the proposed combination of local geometry and the M-Uniform objective as a way to learn useful mesh movement across diverse numerical simulation settings.
neurips-2025-ugm2n-an-unsupervised-and-g.tldr: UGM2N uses local geometry and an unsupervised physics-constrained loss to adapt meshes across different equations, geometries, and resolutions.

paragraphs: Some vision Transformers develop tokens with unusually large activations, producing noisy attention patterns and impairing visual processing. This paper traces that behavior in models including CLIP and DINOv2 to a small set of neurons that concentrate high-norm activations on outlier tokens. That mechanism suggests an intervention for models already trained.

The authors move the large activations from these register neurons into an additional, untrained token. This test-time change mimics the role of learned register tokens without retraining the model from scratch. They also provide a simple mathematical model that reflects the observed relationship between register neurons and high-norm tokens.

The method produces cleaner attention and feature maps, improves over base models on multiple visual tasks, and achieves results comparable to models trained with registers. Applying it to existing vision-language models also improves the clarity of attention-based text-to-image attribution. These results suggest that test-time registers can fulfill the role of trained registers, offering a training-free approach for pretrained models released without them.
neurips-2025-vision-transformers-don-t-n.tldr: Redirecting unusually large activations into an untrained token improves vision Transformer attention maps and downstream results without retraining.

paragraphs: Deep networks predict human eye-movement sequences well, but their decisions can be difficult to interpret. Mechanistic models describe behavior through explicit cognitive mechanisms yet tend to predict less accurately. This paper uses the stronger predictions of DeepGaze III to discover targeted improvements to SceneWalk, an interpretable model of how people look around scenes.

The authors identify individual fixations that DeepGaze III predicts successfully and SceneWalk misses. These discrepancies motivate specific additions to SceneWalk: time-dependent temperature scaling, saccadic momentum, and an adaptive cardinal attention bias. The approach uses disagreements between models to guide the development and testing of interpretable mechanisms for visual behavior.

With these extensions, SceneWalk’s explained variance on MIT1003 increases from 35% to 70%, establishing a new state of the art for mechanistic scanpath prediction. The improvement concerns explained variance on this dataset, giving a precise meaning to the reported doubling. More broadly, the results demonstrate how a high-performing neural model can help develop a more accurate mechanistic account of human behavior.
neurips-2025-what-moves-the-eyes-doublin.tldr: DeepGaze III guides interpretable extensions to SceneWalk that double its explained variance on MIT1003 from 35% to 70%.

paragraphs: A generative model may produce impressive outputs while still making it difficult for a user to obtain the particular result they want. This paper calls that goal-directed capability steerability. It develops a mathematical decomposition that separates steerability from producibility, the quality and range of outputs a model is capable of generating.

Measuring steerability requires knowing the user’s target. The authors create a benchmark by sampling an output from the model and asking users to reproduce it. This supplies a concrete goal that is already within the model’s production capabilities. User studies apply the benchmark to both text-to-image systems and large language models.

All models studied perform poorly on steerability despite producing high-quality outputs. The paper also shows that simple image-based steering mechanisms improve performance by more than twofold on this benchmark. These findings identify a gap between generating good samples and helping users reach intended outcomes, while demonstrating that changes to steering mechanisms can materially improve the measured ability to reach a target.
neurips-2025-what-s-producible-may-not-b.tldr: A reproduction benchmark reveals poor user steerability in tested generative models, with simple image-based mechanisms delivering more than twofold improvement.
